summary.text: 语 is the standardized simplified form of 語, a character for speaking and language. In 語, 言 contributes the speech-related meaning and 吾 serves as a sound element; their reconstructed older pronunciations are similar, though modern Mandarin yǔ and wú differ.

formation.text: The traditional graph 語 is phonosemantic: 言 supplies the speech-related meaning, while 吾 supplies a sound cue. The simplified graph 语 retains that construction, with 言 written in its standardized left-side form 讠. Early bronze forms are reported with differing phonetic shapes, including one resembling a complex 五; that shape’s identity and pronunciation remain uncertain.

components.text: 讠 is the standardized simplified left-side form of 言. In 语 it retains 言’s speech-related meaning; it is not the form used in the traditional graph 語.
吾 is identified as the sound element in traditional 語. An early bronze phonetic shape is also reported to resemble a complex 五, but its identity and relation to 吾 remain uncertain.

sound.text: The Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstructions are similar enough to support a proposed sound relationship, though their notation differs; these are reconstructions, not recorded pronunciations.
The Middle Chinese reconstructions retain a comparison, though the forms differ.
Modern Mandarin readings diverge and do not themselves demonstrate the historical relationship.

history.text: The received traditional analysis writes 語 with 言 and 吾. A graphic-history account reports bronze examples with two phonetic shapes, one resembling a complex 五 and another identified as 吾, and analyzes forms from the Warring States period onward as 言 plus 吾. The selected seal-style drawings show 言 and 吾 separately in modern redrawings; they do not depict the compound or its early inscription forms.
In the standardized simplified graph 语, the left-side 言 is written 讠 under the simplification rule for the 言 radical.

uncertainties.text: The early bronze phonetic shape resembling a complex 五 is reported, but its original identity and pronunciation remain uncertain; the later 吾 analysis and sound comparison do not resolve it.
A proposal derives 言 from 語 with a nominal suffix. The relation remains a proposal.

senses.text: One cited Analects passage uses 語 for speaking or discussing. Its surviving witness is not dated here, so this example does not establish the earliest attested use.

senses.period: dating unresolved; cited in an Analects example
senses.text: A separate cited Analects passage uses 語 for telling or addressing. Its chronological relation to the speak/discuss use is unresolved.
Current dictionary meanings include language, words, saying, and expression. The available examples do not establish when these uses developed in relation to the older speak/discuss and tell uses.

limitations.text: Additional recorded senses include literary wording, signals, and animal calls, but the cited material gives no dated sequence linking them to the speak/discuss, tell, or current meanings.
The surviving witnesses behind the cited historical examples are not dated, and no chronology connecting those uses to the current meanings is established.

overview.text: 语 is the simplified form of 語, a character for speaking and language. In 語, 言 points to speech, while 吾 provides a sound cue; their reconstructed older pronunciations are similar, though modern Mandarin readings differ.

components.text: 讠 is the standardized simplified left-side form of 言 and carries its speech-related meaning.
In traditional 語, 吾 is the sound element. Its older reconstructed pronunciation is similar to 語’s, though their modern readings differ.

relationships.text: 讠 is the standardized simplified left-side form of 言 in 语 and retains its speech-related contribution from traditional 語.

The received analysis identifies 吾 as the sound element in 語. Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstructions for 吾 (*ŋˤa) and 語 (*ŋ(r)aʔ) are similar enough to support a historical phonetic relation, despite differing notation and modern Mandarin readings. A separate early bronze shape resembling a complex 五 is reported, but its identity and relation to 吾 remain unresolved.
语 is the standardized simplified counterpart of 語; the left-side 言 is written 讠 under the simplification rule for that radical.
